feedback: If warning colours are called 'just pretty', re-frame: bright is a message — 'stay away, I might sting or taste bad' — not decoration.
If the hoverfly is said to 'really sting because it has stripes', clarify: it cannot sting; looking dangerous is enough to borrow the protection.
activities.intendedInsight: The three strategies are distinguished by their logic, and warning colours work because a predator often learns to avoid that pattern after a bad experience with it.
learnerActions: Sort a set of insects into three groups: camouflage, warning colours, and mimicry.
Match each mimic to the dangerous model it copies (hoverfly to wasp).
Answer: 'Why do a wasp's bright stripes help it survive?' and justify your choice.
Explain in a sentence why a harmless hoverfly with wasp stripes is still left alone by predators.
activities.title: Sort and explain the strategies

feedback: If the learner thinks predators are 'stupid' to be fooled, reframe: the tricks exploit sensible learning — avoiding things that hurt you is smart.
activities.intendedInsight: Putting the predator's reasoning into words — avoidance often follows a bad experience, and a convincing copy earns the same avoidance.
learnerActions: Interview a bird character: 'Why don't you eat the stripy ones?' and 'Why did you leave the hoverfly alone?'
Press further: 'What happened the first time you tried to eat something stripy?' to surface the learned-avoidance logic.
Use the bird's answers to write or say why each strategy keeps an insect from being eaten.
activities.title: Ask the bird (optional dialogue)
